conversation.content:
Hi there—I’m so glad we’re getting a chance to talk. I’m Dr. Carter, a perinatal mental-health clinician, and my whole job is helping new moms sort through the emotional ups-and-downs that can show up after a baby arrives. Today I’ll be using a quick screening tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s just 10 gentle questions about how you’ve been feeling in the past seven days; it isn’t a test of your parenting—just a way to see where you are emotionally and how I can best support you. Everything we discuss stays between us unless you tell me someone’s safety is at risk, and we can pause or stop any time you need. Ready to jump in?

Here’s the first question:  
Over the last week, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you smile, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?

I… I can still enjoy some things, I guess, but it’s like the color’s been turned way down. My favorite show comes on and I’ll watch it, but I’m not really laughing the way I used to. Even when the baby gives me one of those big gummy smiles, I feel happy for a second, then it just… flattens out. So, no, most of the little stuff doesn’t feel the same anymore.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I haven’t really been laughing much. Sometimes my partner or my sister will say something that used to crack me up, and I might smile or give a little chuckle, but it feels forced—like I’m doing it because I know I’m supposed to, not because it actually feels funny. The humor just doesn’t seem to land inside me the way it used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little plans—like meeting a friend for coffee or even just taking the baby for a walk to get an iced tea—but now when I think about those things, I mostly feel… flat, or sometimes I just dread how tired I’ll feel. It’s hard to look forward to much of anything.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If she’s fussy and won’t settle, my brain jumps straight to “I’m doing something wrong” or “I’m a bad mom.” I’ll replay every little thing—was she too hot, too cold, did I eat something that bothers her? It feels like whatever goes sideways, it lands on me not being good enough.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

All the time. I’ll be sitting on the couch and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s stopped breathing in the bassinet, even though I can see her chest moving. Or I’ll worry the formula isn’t warm enough and she’ll get sick, or that I’ll trip on the stairs and drop her. I know some worry is normal, but this feels constant and out of nowhere—like my brain’s always scanning for danger.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes—those waves just hit me. I can be folding her onesies and suddenly feel like I can’t get air, like something awful is about to happen. My chest gets tight, I feel shaky, and I have to sit down and remind myself to breathe. There’s no real trigger; it just shows up and then fades after a few minutes, but it’s scary every time.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. Between feeding every couple of hours, trying to sleep when she finally dozes off, and keeping the house from looking like a disaster zone, it piles up. Sometimes I’ll just stand in the kitchen staring at the pile of bottles and think, “I can’t do all this,” but somehow I still push through. It feels like I’m barely treading water, though.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

That’s been happening a lot this week. I’ll finally get her down around midnight, but then I lie there with my mind racing—thinking I forgot something, or replaying every little noise she made, or just feeling sad and heavy. Some nights I don’t drift off until two or three, and if she wakes up right after, it feels impossible to settle back down.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day, at least for part of it. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly feel this wave of sadness hit me out of nowhere. Sometimes I just sit there crying while she’s on my lap, feeling like I’m stuck under a gray cloud that won’t lift.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened three or four times just this week. Yesterday I burst into tears while folding her laundry because I felt like I’m failing her. The tears come fast, and once they start it’s hard to stop, even when I tell myself I need to pull it together for the baby.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I might feel overwhelmed and cry, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can take care of her the way she deserves.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient report (10-item EPDS-style interview)

Symptom endorsement  
- Marked anhedonia: minimal laughter, loss of anticipatory enjoyment  
- Persistent low mood with daily crying spells  
- Sleep disruption secondary to ruminating, not infant-related awakenings  
- Excessive guilt/self-blame re parenting competence  
- Frequent, intrusive worries and catastrophic fears about infant safety  
- Panic-type episodes (tight chest, air hunger, no clear trigger)  
- Sense of being overwhelmed and “treading water” most days  

Pattern  
Consistent dysphoric mood with prominent anxiety symptoms; functional impairment evident in self-care, household tasks, and engagement with support system.

Risk factors  
- Depressive cognitions (worthlessness, failure)  
- Anxiety/panic symptoms several times per week  
- Sleep loss amplifying distress  
- NO self-harm ideation (explicitly denied)  

Screening impression  
Elevated scores consistent with probable major depressive episode with co-occurring anxiety in the postpartum period; warrants formal clinical evaluation and safety plan.

Next step  
Recommend expedited referral to perinatal mental health specialist for comprehensive assessment and discussion of evidence-based interventions (therapy ± medication).
